headline: Garden revolutionaries ditch soil for building waste
meta_description: Gardeners are creating drought-tolerant, biodiverse spaces using leftover builders' waste instead of soil. The Horniman Museum in London leads the trend.
summary_short: Forward-thinking gardeners are transforming construction waste into thriving, low-maintenance gardens full of hardy plants and wildlife. Here's how.
body:
If you've been told you need rich soil to grow a garden, think again. Across the UK and beyond, horticulturists and designers are discovering that leftover builders' materials—concrete, gravel, sand—create ideal conditions for drought-resistant plants while solving a waste problem. At London's Horniman Museum, head of horticulture Errol Reuben Fernandes recently transformed the entrance gardens using 25 tonnes of waste concrete aggregate from a path redevelopment. The result: a thriving collection of xerophytes from the Mediterranean, Peru, Chile, Bolivia and Mexico that bloom throughout the seasons, replacing a monoculture that looked bare most of the year. These hardy plants, adapted to extreme climates with hot summers and cold winters, thrive where traditional gardens struggle.

What began as an experiment decades ago—Beth Chatto and Derry Watkins pioneered gravel gardens in the 1990s—is gaining urgent momentum as climate shifts make water conservation essential. The appeal extends beyond aesthetics. Nathan Apperley, head gardener at Yeo Valley Organic in Somerset, sees rubble gardens as a solution to the disheartening reality of new-build homes, where compacted subsoil causes conventional lawns to fail. Instead, rubble gardens attract bees, beetles, spiders and other insects, creating natural ecosystems that need minimal intervention. Even Elizabeth Waddington, a permaculture designer in Scotland, found that waste materials from renovating an old stone barn spontaneously hosted native wildflowers with fewer weeds than expected.

The movement does require a mindset shift. Fernandes acknowledges that a heap of concrete raises eyebrows before planting, but encourages neighbours to understand the vision. The key principle: use waste materials already on-site whenever possible, keeping environmental impact local rather than offsetting it through transportation.
quick_facts: Horniman Museum used 25 tonnes of waste concrete to create diverse xerophyte gardens
Hardy plants from Mediterranean, Peru, Chile, Bolivia and Mexico now thrive at London site
Rubble gardens attract bees, beetles and spiders, creating natural ecosystems
Beth Chatto and Derry Watkins pioneered gravel gardening in the 1990s
Builders often lay lawns over compacted subsoil on new-build homes, causing failure
